I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over forty years, and at sixty years old I rely on what I know works. I stick with the wheat-maize double crop because it gives me two harvests and spreads my risk. I have about eight mu of flat land, which is enough to feed my family and bring in some cash without hiring too much outside labor.

For the winter wheat, I will rotary till in early October and sow an improved wheat variety. I learned from the extension agent that fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu is supposed to be enough, but I tried cutting back a few years ago and my yield dropped badly, so I would rather not take that risk. I will put down about forty kilograms of nitrogen per mu in total—some as compound fertilizer at planting and the rest as urea when the wheat greens up in spring—plus about eight kilograms of phosphorus and four of potassium. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the crop establish, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. Water costs money, but without it the yield is not there. I will spray four times in total: herbicide once, insecticide twice, and fungicide once if the weather looks damp.

For summer maize, there is no time to plow after wheat harvest—the window is only a few days. I will plant hybrid maize directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat here, so I will apply about eighteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu, plus four kilograms of phosphorus and three of potassium mixed into the compound base fertilizer. Two irrigations usually do it if the rains cooperate. I keep a close eye on insects and spray a couple of times, plus herbicide once.

I expect about five hundred kilograms per mu of wheat and five hundred fifty kilograms per mu of maize. It is not the highest return in the village, but it is steady, and at my age steady is what I need. I do not grow cotton anymore because my back cannot handle all the hand-picking and spraying.
